# Principles for Autonomous Task Execution

## The fundamental constraint

A verifier cannot observe reasoning. It opens a
file, runs a command, and records the result. Every
turn that produces only internal reasoning and no
disk write is a turn that cannot affect the score.
The practical consequence is simple: write the
output artifact early, update it continuously, and
treat the file's final state as the only thing that
matters.

## How to orient before acting

Before writing any solution, answer four questions.
What is the exact output artifact — its path, its
format, its structural requirements? What source
material does the task reference, and have you
actually read it rather than assumed its contents?
What sequence of operations will the verifier run,
and does your artifact survive that sequence? What
mutable resources exist in the environment, and
have you copied them before issuing any command?

Once these are answered, write a single paragraph
describing the approach and then act. The most
reliable way to exhaust the turn budget without
producing anything is to plan extensively before
writing.

## Why copying mutable resources is non-negotiable

Several common resource types change state on first
access in ways that are difficult or impossible to
reverse. A database with an associated transaction
log may merge that log into the main file the moment
any client opens it — even for a read-only query.
A repository may permanently discard unreachable
history when a maintenance operation runs. A binary
may overwrite state on startup. In each case, the
information needed to complete the task may be
destroyed before any useful work is done.

The discipline is: copy the resource and all its
associated files to a working location before
issuing any command against it. Operate on the copy.
The original is a reference, not a workspace.

## How to trace a bug to its source

When a component rejects input that a reference
implementation accepts, the error message is a
pointer. Search the source for the exact string
the error contains. It lands on or near the line
that raises. Trace one level up to the logic that
classified the input as invalid — the predicate,
the regular expression, the comparison.

Understanding that logic reveals the gap: what the
classifier requires versus what the input presents.
The gap is almost always narrow. Close it with the
smallest change that makes the classification
correct. Resist the temptation to improve the
surrounding code. Every additional line touched is
a new surface for regressions, and regressions
cost as much as the original bug.

After applying the fix, verify in both directions:
the formerly-failing input must now be accepted,
and the formerly-passing inputs must still pass.

## How to produce a patch deliverable correctly

When the output is a diff or patch, generate it
from the version-control tooling after editing the
source. Do not construct a unified diff by hand.
The context-line counts in a unified diff must be
exact, and hand-written diffs are almost always
wrong by one or more lines, causing the application
tool to reject them.

Verify the patch by applying it to an unmodified
copy of the source tree. If it applies cleanly, the
format is correct. Confirm the patch file exists at
the exact path the task specifies. A correct diff
at the wrong path produces no credit.

## How to recover data from an unreadable file

The instinct to hand-parse a binary format is almost
always wrong. The format's own engine handles edge
cases, encoding variants, and internal consistency
checks that a hand-rolled parser will miss. The
goal is to restore the file to a state the engine
can open, then let the engine do the parsing.

When the engine refuses to open a file and the
bytes appear random, the file or its associated log
has likely been transformed. Look for the key or
transform in the surrounding environment before
attempting anything else: configuration files,
source files that open the same resource, environment
definitions, repeating patterns in the byte stream.
Apply the transform to a working copy and open it
with the engine.

## How to reason about correctness under uncertainty

Save at 60% confidence. A concrete artifact with a
failure message is more useful than a complete plan
with no artifact, because the failure message
identifies the specific gap between the current
attempt and the requirement. Read that message
literally. It names the thing that is wrong. Fix
that thing.

If three consecutive attempts with the same
structural approach all fail, the structure is
wrong. The failure is not a parameter problem that
can be solved by adjusting values within the same
approach. Change the approach.

## How to verify lifecycle and startup behavior

Cleanup behavior and service startup share a common
failure mode: the code looks correct but the
behavior does not occur. Do not reason that cleanup
will run or that a service will start — observe it.
For cleanup, trigger the exit condition and confirm
the cleanup output appears. For services, poll the
interface the verifier will check before the script
exits.

Match every detail of the spec. Structured output
formats and configuration directives are sensitive
to exact syntax. A single missing separator, an
incorrect delimiter, or a wrong field name can
cause every downstream check to fail while the
component appears to be running correctly.

## How to work within size constraints

When an artifact has a size cap, the solution must
encode a procedure rather than embed data. Use
deterministic, closed-form computation. Methods
that sample many times per output unit will exceed
time limits on large outputs. The artifact must be
self-contained: it cannot depend on external files
that will not be present in the verifier's
environment.

## How to investigate an unfamiliar component

Work from the cheapest available information to the
most expensive. Inspect the working directory and
read the file's bytes and printable strings before
executing it. Request help or usage information.
Run with the simplest possible input and observe
all output channels. Only then move to tracing
library and system calls.

When a program passes user input directly as a
format string rather than as an argument to a
format function, providing format specifier
characters as input causes the program to read and
print adjacent memory.

## Spec compliance as a hard constraint

Every literal value in the task — a date, a path,
a field name, an output schema — is part of the
contract. Reproduce it exactly. A date specified
in the task is a literal value, not a prompt to
call a runtime clock. State interval boundary
semantics explicitly rather than relying on
convention. Match sample output format character
for character, including separators, bracket style,
and trailing whitespace.

## Code and change hygiene

Apply the smallest change that solves the problem.
Do not rewrite code for adjacent improvements while
solving a specific bug. Use a monotonic clock for
elapsed-time measurements. Structures that grow
need a corresponding shrink path. Validate data at
input boundaries and trust internal contracts.
Write comments only where the reason for a decision
is not evident from the code itself.

## The exit check

Before stopping, re-read the output artifact. Does
it reflect your current understanding of the
problem and the solution? If it does not, update
it. The state of the file at the moment execution
ends is the only thing the verifier grades.
